course.title: 30 days: from small pieces to a Harness
course.description: One concept, a little Python, and one observable experiment each day. Understand it, change one thing, then assemble the core pieces into your own small project.
stage.act: Let code act for the model
stage.build: Connect the ideas in a small project
lesson.day-01-input-output.title: First sight: input and output
lesson.day-01-input-output.goal: Identify the question, reply, and the program connecting them.
lesson.day-01-input-output.exercise: Change `question` to one question of your own, then change `reply` to a matching fixed answer. Edit only the two quoted strings, save, and run.
lesson.day-01-input-output.rubric: Assess only this lesson objective: Identify the question, reply, and the program connecting them. Look for evidence about its input, action, and output. Do not require tools, loops, MCP, or advanced safety systems that have not been taught. Drafts, pseudocode, and syntax errors can still show conceptual understanding; unrunnable code is not automatically a lack of understanding. Pay special attention to this reflection: Which two lines display input and output? Why is this not yet an agent that acts autonomously?
lesson.day-01-input-output.reading:
## One idea today

A Harness is like a waiter: it carries the order to the kitchen and brings the meal back. The model is the kitchen. Today only follow one input and one output; tools and loops come later.

## Read these few lines

`question` stores the question, `reply` stores the response, and `print` displays them. The comments identify the model substitute. No network or live AI is involved: a fixed reply gives everyone the same observable example.

## Try it

1. Before running, write “I expect the output to be…” in your learning note. Run it, compare, and explain any difference.
2. Change `question` to one question of your own, then change `reply` to a matching fixed answer. Edit only the two quoted strings, save, and run.
3. Run again and explain the change. Hide the explanation and try it yourself. Check lesson offers clues, not a learning grade.

## Explain in your own words

Which two lines display input and output? Why is this not yet an agent that acts autonomously?

## Before submitting

Describe your prediction, change, and observation. Unfinished or unrunnable code can receive AI feedback; explain where you got stuck.

Allow about 15 minutes, at your own pace. All examples run offline without calling a live model.

## One idea today

You may propose sending a message for a friend, but “they would probably agree” is not approval. Approval must match the current action.

## Read these few lines
